title_content.content: Modular assembly of complex C-alkyl glycoside enabled via cooperative NHC and photoredox catalysis

paragraph_content.content: Rui-Qiang Jiao<sup>1</sup>, Ming Li<sup>2</sup>, Xi Chen<sup>1</sup>, Mei-Ze Xu<sup>1</sup>, Tian Ding<sup>1</sup>, Xiao-Ping Gong<sup>1</sup>, Zhuo-Mei Li<sup>1</sup>, Xue-Yuan Liu<sup>1*</sup> & Yong-Min Liang<sup>1</sup>

<sup>1</sup>State Key Laboratory of Applied Organic Chemistry, Lanzhou University, Lanzhou 730000, China <sup>2</sup>College of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Northwest Normal University, Lanzhou 730070, China
Received July 31, 2024; accepted October 8, 2024; published online January 2, 2025

C-Alkyl glycosides are found in natural products and are indispensable in drug development programs, owing to their diverse range of medicinal properties. Two-component reactions involving glycosyl radical addition are well documented and proved efficient for the C-alkyl glycosides synthesis. However, multicomponent reactions for the rapid and controllable construction of structurally diversified C-alkyl glycosides in a single step remains a significant challenge due to the issues associated with balancing reactivity, compatibility, and selectivity. Herein, we report an NHC and photoredox co-catalyzed three-component method to access complex and valuable C-alkyl glycosides. This protocol exhibits broad substrate scope and excellent chemoand regioselectivity. Furthermore, nine types of sugars are compatible with this reaction. In addition, the generality of this catalytic strategy was further highlighted by the potential for scalable production, the feasibility of further modifications of the products and its successful application in the late-stage functionalization of pharmaceutical skeletons.
C-alkyl glycosides, three-component, NHC catalysis, visible-light photoredox catalysis, radical-radical coupling

Citation: Jiao RQ, Li M, Chen X, Xu MZ, Ding T, Gong XP, Li ZM, Liu XY, Liang YM. Modular assembly of complex C-alkyl glycoside enabled via cooperative NHC and photoredox catalysis. Sci China Chem, 2025, 68: 1412–1417, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11426-024-2348-y

C-Alkylglycosides are an important class of carbohydrate scaffolds that are prevalent structural motifs in biologically relevant molecules as key structural elements (Scheme 1a) [1]. Compared with O-glycosides, their stability in vitro and in vivo is obviously enhanced, which plays an important role in the modern design of C-glycoside drug candidates and studies of important biological processes [2].

Considering the important biological activity and medical value of C-alkylglycosides, as such, the development of synthetic methods for C-alkylglycosides is an unmet need for organic chemists. The generation of glycosyl radical intermediates provides an efficient strategy for the synthesis ofCglycosides [3–10]. Among those approaches, the addition of glycosyl radicals across alkenes has evolved to a key strategy for the synthesis of C-alkylglycosides (Scheme 1b) [3,7–10]. Inspired by Giese’s pioneering work [9a] on the use of tributyltin hydride under photolysis conditions, so far, many research groups have explored the Sn- [9a,9e], Et B-[9m,9n], AIBN- [9h], or Sm-mediated [7a,7c,7d] and Ni-[9f], Ru- [9j,9i], Fe- [9o], or Ti-catalyzed [9l] Giese reactions for C-alkylglycosides. These reactions, which can be conducted under practical and mild conditions, feature high functional group tolerance and broad substrate scope. Recently, Hu’s group [11] realized the synthesis of gem-difluoroalkene-containing C-alkylglycosides via a photomediated defluorinative gem-difluoroallylation reaction. Very recently, our group reported the synthesis C-alkyl glycosides of α-aryl-β-glycosamide via Smiles rearrangement [12]. Despite the significant progress recorded in this field, the intermolecular three-component cascade reactions for molecular complexity C-alkylglycosides synthesis has been far less developed. There is only one example, in 2023, Ackermann’s group [13] achieved a domino meta-C–H ethylglycosylation by merging the addition of glycosyl radicals to olefins and ruthenium catalysis for distal C–H activation three-component radical cross-coupling reactions. As a result, the development of a new method involving the glycosyl radical intermolecular three-component cascade reactions for complex molecules C-alkylglycosides synthesis is greatly desired.

paragraph_content.content: In recent years, the combination of visible light and NHC cocatalyzed radical coupling reactions has generated recent excitement to drive complex bond constructions. The key step ofthe reaction is radical and ketyl radical cross-coupling delivers a ketone-containing product. So far, many elegant works have been well-established by Ohmiya and other groups [14]. On the other hand, 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes via a radical pathway has also been intensively investigated recently [15]. However, NHC-promoted radical 1,4-difunctionalization of1,3-enynes remains a challenge for the synthesis of functionalized allenes ketones. Du [16], Huang [17], Hong [18] and Zhang et al. [19] independently developed a NHC-promoted radical 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes, providing a ready access to different substituted allenyl ketones. Despite significant progress, it is surprising to observe that NHC-promoted radical 1,4-glycosylacylation of 1,3-enynes has not yet been explored. Considering the importance of the complex molecules Calkylglycosides in medicinal chemistry and inspired by previous work, we wondered whether the combination of glycosyl radical addition and NHC and photoredox catalysis could be feasible for modular assembly of complex C-alkylglycosides. With our group’s ongoing research on Cglycosylation, herein, we report an NHC and photoredox cocatalyzed three-component reaction from readily available 1,3-enynes, aroyl fluorides, glycosyl bromides. This transformation involves the coupling of ketyl radical from single electron transfer (SET) reduction of in situ formed acylazolium ions and allenyl radical from glycosyl radicals selectively attacks the olefin unit of the 1,3-enyne to produce the propargyl radical intermediate, which could undergo reversible resonance, providing direct access to an array of complex and structurally diversified valuable C-alkyl glycosides under mild, transition-metal-free conditions.

In a 10 mL pre-dried schlenk tube with stir bar, (TMS) SiOH (39 mg, 0.15 mmol, 1.5 equiv.), glycosylbromide 2a (0.25 mmol, 2.5 equiv.), PC1 (4.2 mg, 3 mol%), NHC-A (8.3 mg, 20 mol%), and K CO (41.4 mg, 0.3 mmol, 3.0 equiv.) were added. The tube was charged with argon, which repeated more than three times. Subsequently, 1 mL MeCN was injected and 1a (0.1 mmol) and 3a (0.2 mmol) were added. Then the reaction mixture was irradiated with blue light-emitting diode (LED) at room temperature for 12 h. After the reaction completed, the solvent was evaporated under vacuum. The residue was purified by flash chromatography on silica gel (petroleum ether/ethyl acetate = 3:1) to afford the corresponding product 4a.

Screening of photosensitizers showed that 4-BrCZIPN exhibited the highest yield (entries 2–4). When the reducing agent was (TMS) SiH, the yield down to 40% (entry 5). It should be mentioned that the solvent could be the key factor in this catalytic system to control the yield, and no product was observed with dimethyl formamide (DMF), dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (entries 6– 7). Replacing

with other bases led to sharply lower yields (entries 8–10). When other NHC precursors were used, the yield of 4a decreased substantially (entries 11–13). Control experiments showed that reducing agent (TMS) - SiOH, photosensitizer, NHC catalyst, light and argon were crucial to the reaction (entries 14–17).

Having established the optimal reaction conditions, and considering the diversity of C-glycosides, pyranose and furanose bromide substrates were then investigated. As shown Table 2, both pyranoses and furanoses could give the corresponding allenyl ketone in medium to good yields. Glucopyranoses and galactopyranoses, which protected by different substituents, such as acetoxyl (4a and 4c) and benzoyl (4b and 4d) groups, were well-tolerated to this protocol, affording the desired products in yields ranging from 48% to 70%. The L-arabinose generated product 4e in 51% yield with the mixed configuration. The reaction of Dxylose also proceeded smoothly to give products 4f in 40% yield. The protocol could also well accommodate L-rhamnose, and the target products were isolated in 53%–60% yield (4g, 4h). Then we explored D-mannofuranose, delivering the desired products 4i. D-Mannopyranoses was also examined and gave the corresponding product (4j, 4k) in 47%–54% yield. In addition, this reaction also showed good compatibility toward disaccharides (cellubiose and maltose), and the desired product were obtained in 60%–62% yield (4l, 4m).

We subsequently investigated the generality of 1,3-enynes. As shown in Table 3, 1,3-enynes bearing electron-donating (–OMe, –Me) or -withdrawing substituents (–F, Cl, Br) at the para-positions of the 2-phenyl rings (5a–5e) exhibited good reactivity and promoted reactions smoothly in good yields (56%–68%). The substituents at the ortho-position or metaposition also worked well to provide the target product (5f– 5i) in moderate to good yields (53%–67%). Furthermore, substrates with 1-naphthalene and heterocycles were also amenable to this catalytic process and afforded the desired products (5j, 5k) in comparable yields. Besides, 2-alkyl substituted 1,3-enynes were applicable, giving the desired products (5l).

We also explored the scope of acyl fluorides. As shown in Table 4, The electron-donating groups at the aromatic ring’s para-, meta-, or ortho-position reacted efficiently to furnish the corresponding products under these reaction conditions in 65%–72% yields (6a, 6b, 6e, 6g), while the electronwithdrawing groups at the aromatic ring’s para- or orthoposition led to low efficiency (6c, 6d, 6f). Furthermore, multi-substituted aryl acyl fluorides were also tolerated and delivered the expected products 6h in yields of 62%. Substrates with 2-naphthalene moieties could also give the desired products in 51% yield 6i. Additionally, to our surprise, heterocycles like thiophene, furan and pyridine, which have frequently been found in medicinal chemistry due to their various biological activities, were found to be compatible with the reaction conditions (6j–6l).

To further demonstrate the potential synthetic application of this protocol, this approach is also applicable to the latestage drug derivative. Gratifyingly, various drugs/drug fragments linking molecules were successfully functionalized (Scheme 2a), which gave the corresponding products (6m–6p) in 24%–56% yield. We also conducted scale-up synthesis and further chemical transformations of the products (Scheme 2b). The target product (4a) was obtained in 57% yield when the reaction was expanded to the 2.0 mmol level and the ketone unit of 4a can be reduced by NaBH . In addition, the bromo-containing product 5e could undergo palladium-catalyzed Suzuki coupling with 1-cyclopentenylboronic acid to deliver product 6r (Scheme 2c).

paragraph_content.content: Next, we turned our attention to the mechanism of this transformation. In order to confirm whether radicals were involved, 2,6,6-tetramethyl-1-piperidinyloxy (TEMPO) as a radical scavenger was added under the standard reaction conditions. It was found that the formation of 4a was completely suppressed, which indicated that a radical mechanism might be involved in this transformation. From this reaction mixture, the adducts of TEMPO with glycosy and ketyl radical were detected by high resolution mass spectrum (HRMS, Figure 1a). paragraph_content.content: radical pathway. On the basis of the above results and literature reports, a plausible reaction mechanism for the modular assembly of complex C-alkyl glycoside is proposed in (Figure 1b). Initially, the (TMS) SiO anion, which comes from (TMS) SiOH in the presence of
undergoes single-electron oxidation by the excited 4-BrCZIPN* to afford the
\mathrm { ( T M S ) } _ { 3 } \mathrm { S i O }

radical. Subsequently, the (TMS) SiO radical spontaneously turns into the (TMS) (TMSO)Si<sup>·</sup> radical by Brook rearrangement. Next, glycosyl radical C is generated from radical transfer between (TMS) (TMSO)Si and glycosyl bromide 1a, and it selectively attacks the olefin unit of the 1,3-enyne 2a to produce the propargyl radical intermediate D, which could undergo reversible resonance to generate relatively stable allenyl radical E. The acyl fluoride 3a could react with NHCs produces the acylazolium intermediate A, which can be reduced by 4-BrCZIPN species to provide ketyl radical B and regenerate the ground state 4- BrCZIPN photocatalyst. The coupling of E with radical B ultimately yields the target product 4a and releases the NHCs catalyst.

In summary, we have developed a strategy to accomplish multicomponent assembly of complex C-alkyl glycoside via cooperative NHC and photoredox catalysis under mild, transition-metal-free conditions. This multicomponent coupling reaction used readily available starting materials with broad functional group compatibility and excellent chemoand regionselectivity. Mechanistic studies suggest that this transformation proceeds via radical/radical cross coupling of ketyl radicals with allenyl radicals. The ketyl radicals are generated via SET reduction of in situ formed acylazolium ions whereas the allenyl radicals derive from chemo-specific glycosyl radical addition to the 1,3-enynes. We expect that this protocol will provide a versatile platform for the multicomponent assembly of complex C-alkyl glycosides and believe this work will stimulate more research in multicomponent reactions for the preparation of structurally diversified valuable C-alkyl glycosides that are difficult-tomade in future.
